planRationale: Rising electricity costs touch nearly every household, and in October 2026 a wave of surveys, Fed/grid-operator projections, and new state laws made the AI-data-center-to-your-bill connection front-page news — yet the site has nothing explaining this cost of AI to everyday readers. It's a concrete, pocketbook topic that a smart non-technical audience cares about now and that will remain relevant for well over a month as grids strain and more states legislate. It also fills a real gap: existing nodes cover model cost and hardware, but none explain AI's energy footprint in human terms.

findings.claim: Tech companies are now racing to secure nuclear power deals just to keep their servers running.
findings.issue: Accurate and well-supported (Microsoft/Constellation Sept 2024, Google/Kairos and Amazon/X-energy Oct 2024, Meta/Constellation June 2025, etc.), but the present-tense 'now' carries no explicit date. It reads as a general ongoing trend rather than an 'as of <date>' snapshot, so it does not trigger the blocking date rule, but adding a year would future-proof it.

findings.claim: Training a model like GPT-4 reportedly consumed around 50-60 gigawatt-hours.
findings.issue: Supported (MIT Technology Review cites ~50 GWh; detailed estimates range ~52-62 GWh). Worth knowing this is an estimate based on leaked specs, not an official OpenAI figure, and GPT-4 is a 2023 model used here only as a historical illustration — which is acceptable framing.

items.note: Upload this single file to content/articles/. The existing indexing.yml workflow rebuilds articles_index.json automatically, and the article becomes visible on /trends within a minute or two.

findings.claim: Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas published in August 2026 found that AI data centers have already pushed average wholesale electricity prices 2% to 6% higher nationwide
findings.issue: The 2%-6% and 20%-30%-by-2028 figures match the widely-reported Dallas Fed findings and are fine. However, the paper itself (Working Paper No. 2606, 'Processing Power: The Effect of Data Centers on Wholesale Electricity Markets') is dated March 20, 2026 (revised October 2026); 'August 2026' is when the major media coverage appeared, not the publication date. Consider rephrasing to 'Dallas Fed research widely reported in August 2026' to avoid mislabeling the publication date.

findings.claim: New York passed legislation in 2026 imposing a moratorium on new data center permits and directing the Public Service Commission to create a separate utility rate class for large data centers.
findings.issue: The New York State Legislature did pass the Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) on June 4, 2026, which includes both provisions as described. However, listing it alongside the fully-enacted NJ and WI measures slightly overstates its status: at least one source indicates the bill had not yet been delivered to or signed by the Governor as of mid-2026, so it may not have been enacted law. Separately, New York did impose a statewide moratorium via executive order (EO 62, 50 MW+). The 'passed legislation' framing is defensible (the legislature did pass it) but the enacted-vs-pending status is worth confirming before presenting it as settled alongside active laws.
